description: God as creator in Genesis and John 1; the Fall, original sin, evil and the problem of suffering.
content_html:
God as Creator

Christians believe that God created the universe and everything in it. The two primary sources for this belief are Genesis 1–3 and the opening of John’s Gospel. Together they present creation as a deliberate act of a loving, purposeful God.

In Genesis chapter 1, God creates the world in six days and declares it “very good.” The Spirit of God hovers over the waters in Genesis 1:2, showing the Holy Spirit’s role as the agent of creation alongside the Father. Human beings are created last and given dominion over the earth, made in God’s image (imago Dei). God rests on the seventh day — establishing Shabbat — and the pattern of creation-rest reflects an ordered, intentional universe.

In John 1, creation is framed through the concept of the Word (Logos): “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was with God in the beginning. Through him all things were made.” John identifies this Word as Jesus, linking him to creation before his birth and establishing his pre-existence. The Apostles’ Creed affirms this: God is “maker of heaven and earth.”

Paul writes in Romans 1:20 that God’s “eternal power and divine nature” are visible through what has been made — a text that underpins natural theology (the argument that creation itself reveals God).

Key Fact

In Christian belief, creation involves all three persons of the Trinity: God the Father as creator, the Holy Spirit as the agent hovering over the waters (Genesis 1:2), and the Word (Jesus, John 1) as the one through whom all things were made. Creation is therefore a Trinitarian act.

Christians differ significantly on how to read Genesis 1–3. A literal interpretation treats the account as historical fact: the world was created in six 24-hour days, a few thousand years ago. This view is associated with Young Earth Creationism and is held by many conservative Evangelical Christians who believe the Bible is the inerrant word of God.

By contrast, a metaphorical interpretation treats Genesis as theological poetry rather than science. Most mainstream Catholic, Anglican and liberal Protestant theologians hold this view, arguing that Genesis teaches who created the world and why (God, for a purpose), not how or when. This allows them to accept the scientific consensus on evolution and the age of the universe without conflict with their faith.

The Fall and Original Sin

The Fall is described in Genesis 3:1–19. Adam and Eve, tempted by the serpent, eat the fruit God had forbidden. As a result, they are expelled from the Garden of Eden, experience shame, and must live with pain, toil and death. Christians interpret this as the first misuse of Free Will — the freedom God gave human beings, which they used against his command.

The Fall gives rise to the doctrine of original sin. Developed by Augustine of Hippo (354–430 CE), this teaching holds that the sin of Adam has been passed down to every human being. No one is born morally neutral — all inherit a bias towards self-interest and away from God. This is why Christians believe they need salvation: without God’s intervention, sin dominates human life.

The Lord’s Prayer in Matthew 6 reflects awareness of this: it includes a petition to be forgiven sins and to be delivered from evil, suggesting that the ongoing reality of sin and temptation is something Christians must regularly bring before God.

Key Fact

The Fall (Genesis 3:1–19) describes Adam and Eve disobeying God, misusing Free Will. Augustine developed the doctrine of original sin from this: all humans inherit a tendency towards sin from Adam. This is why Christians believe the whole of humanity needs saving by Christ.

Types of Evil and Suffering

The existence of evil and suffering is one of the hardest challenges for Christian belief in a loving, all-powerful God. Theologians distinguish two types:

Moral evil arises from the free choices of human beings. When people choose to harm others, lie, exploit or oppress, they cause moral evil. Christians see this as the direct result of the Fall: human Free Will, given by God so that love could be genuine, has been used to cause immense suffering.

Natural evil arises from natural processes — earthquakes, disease, floods, cancer — without any human choice behind them. This kind of suffering is more difficult to explain, since it does not obviously result from human sin.

The problem of evil and suffering asks: if God is omnipotent (able to prevent evil), omniscient (aware of it) and benevolent (willing to prevent it), why does evil exist? This challenge is called the ‘inconsistent triad’.

Christians offer several responses. One is the Free Will defence: God gave humans freedom to love or reject him; removing evil would mean removing freedom. Another is that suffering can produce spiritual growth and character. The book of Job explores a different angle: Job suffers despite being righteous, and God’s response from the whirlwind stresses the limits of human understanding. Some Christians point to Romans 8, which teaches that present suffering “is not worth comparing” with future glory. Others simply acknowledge the mystery — that God’s ways are beyond full human comprehension.
exam_tip_html: For ‘Explain’ questions on creation or the Fall, always link to a named biblical source — for example, “Genesis 3:1–19 describes the Fall when Adam and Eve disobeyed God.” Avoid vague references like “in the Bible it says.” For the 15-mark ‘Discuss’ on evil and suffering, the examiner expects you to present the problem clearly (omnipotent + benevolent + evil = contradiction), give Christian responses to it, and weigh which response is most convincing — all with a justified conclusion. Distinguish clearly between natural evil (earthquakes, disease) and moral evil (human choices): confusing them is a common error that loses marks. Accurate spelling of ‘omnipotent’, ‘omniscient’, ‘original sin’ and ‘benevolent’ is important in the extended response where SPaG is assessed.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christians believe God created the universe through all three persons of the Trinity: Father, Spirit (Genesis 1:2) and the Word/Jesus (John 1); Genesis is interpreted literally by some Christians and metaphorically by others.
  • The Fall (Genesis 3:1–19) describes the first misuse of Free Will and led to Augustine’s doctrine of original sin: all humans inherit a tendency towards sin, making salvation necessary.
  • Christians distinguish moral evil (caused by human choice) from natural evil (caused by natural processes); the problem of evil asks how an omnipotent, benevolent God can allow both — a question Christians answer through the Free Will defence, the example of Job, and trust in God’s purpose.

practice_questions.text: State what Christians mean by 'original sin'.
practice_questions.marks: The idea that all humans inherit a tendency towards sin from Adam / humans are born with a bias towards sin / sin passed down from the Fall. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between natural evil and moral evil.
practice_questions.marks: Natural evil: evil caused by natural events such as earthquakes, disease or floods, not by human choice. [1 mark] Moral evil: evil caused by the free choices of human beings, such as war, murder or cruelty. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline the role of the Word in John 1.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks from: the Word (Logos) was with God and was God from the beginning [1]; all things were made through the Word [1]; John identifies the Word as Jesus [1]; this establishes Jesus's pre-existence as divine before his birth [1].

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Christian responses to the problem of evil and suffering.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- The Free Will defence: God gave humans genuine freedom; to prevent evil would remove the freedom that makes love possible. The Fall (Genesis 3:1-19) shows how Free Will was first misused, but God did not override it. [up to 3 marks]
- The example of Job: the book of Job shows that suffering can be beyond human understanding; God's response from the whirlwind stresses that his purposes are greater than what humans can see. [up to 3 marks]
- Suffering leads to spiritual growth; some Christians argue natural evil and suffering build character and deepen faith.
- The Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:9-15) includes a petition for forgiveness and deliverance from evil, suggesting God hears and responds to suffering. [3 marks per point: 1 simple, 2 developed, 3 developed with source]

practice_questions.text: 'The existence of natural evil makes it impossible to believe in an all-powerful, loving God.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- Natural evil (earthquakes, cancer, floods) is not caused by human Free Will, so the Free Will defence does not explain it.
- If God is omnipotent he could prevent natural disasters; if he is benevolent he would want to. The fact that he does not creates a logical problem.
- The suffering of innocent children (e.g. from disease) seems incompatible with a perfectly loving God.

Arguments against / alternative views:
- The Free Will defence addresses moral evil, but many Christians argue natural evil may serve purposes humans cannot fully see (Romans 8).
- The book of Job shows that suffering can occur without being punishment; God's ways are beyond human comprehension.
- Some Christians take a metaphorical view of Genesis and see the natural world as still 'very good' in its overall design, even if individual events cause suffering.
- Natural evil may be a consequence of the Fall on creation as a whole (the ‘cosmic fall’ interpretation), not a separate problem.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Genesis 3, book of Job, Romans 8); explicit weighing with a justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Both sides present with at least one source; conclusion reached.
Developing: One side stronger; limited sources; conclusion present but not fully weighed.
Emerging: One-sided or brief; no real use of sources; no justified conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Describe two different Christian interpretations of the Genesis creation account.
practice_questions.marks: Literal interpretation: Genesis is historically and scientifically accurate; the world was created in six 24-hour days. [1 mark] Metaphorical interpretation: Genesis is theological poetry conveying who created the world and why, not how or when; science and faith are compatible. [1 mark]

right: Inherited tendency towards sin from Adam
Adam and Eve's disobedience in Genesis 3
Evil caused by natural events not human choice

flashcard_questions.q: What role does the Holy Spirit play in the Genesis creation account?
flashcard_questions.a: The Spirit hovers over the waters as the agent of God's creative power (Genesis 1:2).

flashcard_questions.q: What does John 1 say about Jesus and creation?
flashcard_questions.a: All things were made through the Word (Jesus); he was with God from the beginning.

flashcard_questions.q: What is meant by the pre-existence of Jesus?
flashcard_questions.a: Jesus existed as the divine Word before his birth in Bethlehem.
Adam and Eve's disobedience of God in Genesis 3, bringing sin and death into the world.
The idea that all humans inherit a tendency towards sin from Adam (Augustine).
Evil caused by human choices, such as war, murder or cruelty.
Evil caused by natural events such as earthquakes, disease or floods.
The question of how an omnipotent, benevolent God can allow evil and suffering to exist.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Bible book explores suffering through the story of a righteous man who suffers?
What is a literal interpretation of Genesis?
flashcard_questions.a: Reading it as historically accurate: the world was created in six 24-hour days.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a metaphorical interpretation of Genesis?
flashcard_questions.a: Reading it as theological poetry about who created the world and why, not how or when.

glossary_terms.definition: The first three chapters of the Bible, describing the creation of the world and the origins of human sin.
The first chapter of John's Gospel, which identifies Jesus as the Word (Logos) who was with God from the beginning and through whom all things were made.
The Greek word Logos, meaning Word; in John 1 it refers to the divine reason and creative power of God that became flesh in Jesus.
The existence of Jesus as divine before his birth in Bethlehem; the idea that as the eternal Son of God, he existed before time.
The account in Genesis 3 of Adam and Eve disobeying God by eating the forbidden fruit, bringing sin and death into the world.
The ability to make genuine choices; the capacity to choose between good and evil without being compelled.
The idea, developed especially by Augustine, that all humans inherit a tendency towards sin from Adam, making moral failure a universal human condition.
Reading the Genesis creation account as historically and scientifically accurate: the world was created in six 24-hour days.
Reading the Genesis creation account as symbolic or poetic, conveying theological truths about God's relationship with creation rather than scientific facts.
Evil caused by human choices, such as war, murder, theft and cruelty.
Evil caused by the natural world rather than by human choice, such as earthquakes, disease, floods and tsunamis.
The philosophical question of how an all-powerful, all-knowing and all-loving God can allow evil and suffering to exist.
